sum: Britain’s blue-chip index rose 0.4% on Friday, finishing a 2.2% weekly gain as insurers, utilities and oil majors offset another sell-off in US technology stocks and a global Microsoft outage that disrupted UK public services.

The FTSE 100 closed up 39.47 points, or 0.4%, at 10,902.56 on Friday 13 November 2026, its highest closing level in three months. The index finished the week 2.2% higher, building on Thursday’s 0.25% gain to 10,863.09, which had been helped by data showing the UK economy grew at its fastest pace in two years in the third quarter.

The domestically focused FTSE 250 did not share in the gains, slipping about 0.5% on the day. That divergence is telling: the blue-chip index was carried by large, internationally diversified defensive and commodity names, while mid-caps more exposed to UK borrowing costs struggled as gilt yields rose alongside US Treasuries.

London’s small weighting in technology was once again its biggest advantage. While the Nasdaq Composite fell sharply and chip stocks such as AMD, Broadcom and Intel lost between 5% and 9%, the FTSE 100 is dominated by banks, insurers, energy producers, miners, pharmaceuticals and consumer staples. On a day when investors were rotating out of AI-linked growth stocks and into defensive sectors, that mix was close to ideal.

The dominant story of the session was the abrupt exit of Jensen Huang, the co-founder who had led Nvidia since 1993. The company said on Thursday that he had stepped down as president, chief executive and board member with immediate effect, following reports of multiple affairs, including one with a woman US intelligence suspects of spying for China. Chief financial officer Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO, Harvey C. Jones becomes the company’s first independent chairman, and Nvidia is due to report quarterly results next week. Nvidia shares opened as much as 14% lower on Thursday before closing down 4.34%, and extended losses on Friday after HSBC downgraded the stock.

For London, the Huang story was less a direct hit than a sentiment shock. Analysts at Quilter Cheviot noted that the immediate impact on Nvidia’s order book may be limited, but warned that the episode could damage the wider AI ecosystem over a longer horizon.

Акции розничной торговли подскочили, акции домостроительной компании Taylor Wimpey упали, а в тот же день должны быть опубликованы данные по ВВП Великобритании.

Индекс FTSE 100 был настроен на осторожное, немного более мягкое открытие в Лондоне в четверг, 12 ноября 2026 года, поскольку устойчивая инфляция в США подтолкнула инвесторов обратно к взгляду на процентные ставки «выше и дольше».

Октябрьский отчет по индексу потребительских цен США (ИПЦ) показал, что основные цены выросли на 0,4% в месячном исчислении. Базовый индекс потребительских цен, не учитывающий продукты питания и энергию, вырос на 0,3%.
Эти показатели, наряду с продолжающимся давлением на услуги и транспорт, усилили ожидания того, что Федеральная резервная система будет сохранять жесткую политику и поддерживать доллар.
Ожидания более высоких процентных ставок в США, как правило, приводят к росту доходности мировых облигаций. Это повышает стоимость заимствований как для правительств, так и для компаний.

sum: The Morning Bull — утренний обзор рынка Великобритании, четверг, 12 ноября 2026 г.

Рынок акций Великобритании настроен на осторожное, немного более мягкое открытие, при этом настроения зависят от одного выпуска. Устойчивая инфляция в США подталкивает инвесторов обратно к мышлению о более высоких и более долгосрочных ставках во всем мире.

Октябрьский отчет по индексу потребительских цен в США показал, что основные цены выросли на 0,4% в месячном исчислении, а базовый индекс потребительских цен вырос на 0,3%. Эти показатели, наряду с постоянным давлением на услуги и транспорт, усилили ожидания того, что Федеральная резервная система сохранит жесткую политику и поддержку доллара.

Этот фон имеет значение для рынков Великобритании, поскольку ожидания более высоких процентных ставок в США, как правило, приводят к росту глобальной доходности, повышая стоимость заимствований для правительств и компаний. Укрепившийся доллар также может оказывать давление на фунт стерлингов, что отражается на структурах импортируемых затрат и доходах, переводимых из-за границы.

Ключевой вопрос сейчас заключается в том, как долго продлится эта инфляционная устойчивость. Предстоящие заявки на пособие по безработице в США и серия выступлений ФРС могут либо ужесточить мнение рынка о расширенной жесткой политике, либо вновь открыть дверь для более мягкой политики ставок.

Индийская таможня конфисковала более 40 контейнеров шотландского виски Diageo в споре по поводу 150-процентной импортной пошлины на оптовые концентраты. Разногласия зависят от того, распространяется ли торговое соглашение между Великобританией и Индией на эти поставки или только на готовые спиртные напитки в бутылках. Инвесторы будут следить за любой резолюцией, которая прояснит тарифный режим и восстановит нормальные потоки на этот важный рынок.

Управление по конкуренции и рынкам Великобритании выразило серьезную обеспокоенность по поводу предлагаемого слияния McCormick и продовольственного подразделения Unilever стоимостью от 44,8 до 65 миллиардов долларов. Регуляторы видят потенциальную угрозу конкуренции в сухих кулинарных смесях и соусах. Unilever планирует продать бренд Colman и должна до 18 ноября предложить средства правовой защиты, в противном случае сделка может перейти на вторую фазу рассмотрения.

items.t: Подходящее ли сейчас время для покупки акций Legal & General или их продажи?
sum: Investors aren't totally convinced by Legal & General (LSE: LGEN) shares. I hold this FTSE 100 insurer and asset manager, and I'm not completely convinced either. From time to time, I've even been tempted to sell. So far, I've clung on. Is that loyalty justified, or am I simply refusing to admit I've backed the wrong horse?

There's one thing investors will be happy with: income. Legal & General has one of the highest yields on the FTSE 100, currently 7.15% on a trailing basis. Reinvesting that income could double an investment in roughly 10 years, even if the shares go nowhere. If they rise, so much the better.

The board plans to increase dividends by 2% a year, giving forecast yields of 7.29% in 2026 and 7.44% in 2027. That's generous, but those increases are below inflation, meaning the real value of the income will gradually shrink.

The real frustration is the share price. Legal & General has spent the past dozen years going nowhere. It's a complicated business and questions over the quality of earnings have all weighed on sentiment.
Asset management profits were broadly flat in 2025, while its Solvency II coverage ratio fell from 232% to 210%, partly reflecting asset revaluations and shareholder returns.

Yet the business is improving. Core operating profit rose 6% in 2025 to £1.62bn, with core earnings per share (EPS) up 9%. In the first half of 2026, operating profit grew another 7% and EPS climbed 11%.
The shares have responded, climbing 28% over the past year. Add the dividend and the total return is closer to 35%.

items.t: 22 года роста дивидендов! Это лучшая акция с пассивным доходом из индекса FTSE 100?
sum: Targeting FTSE 100 stocks can be a brilliant strategy for those aiming for long-term passive income. Dividends are never, ever guaranteed. Yet many blue-chip UK shares have the kind of sturdy business models and balance sheets that support large and growing shareholder payouts.
Many Footsie shares have raised dividends strongly since the global pandemic of 2020. Some have exceptional records of payout growth dating back 10 years or more.
And then there's those superstars that have grown dividends consistently for decades. BAE Systems (LSE:BA.) is one such passive income share I want to talk about today.
Dividends here have risen for 22 years on the spin. And if City analysts are correct, the company's on course to reach a quarter of a century of uninterrupted dividend growth in 2028.
The question is, does this make BAE the ultimate FTSE 100 income stock?
Perhaps. Perhaps not. It depends on whether you happen to prize dividend growth over near-term dividend yields.

Let me explain. BAE Systems' share price has soared 250% over the past three years, driven by surging defence spending by major customers including the US Department of Defence and the British government.

sum: London stocks were set to tumble at the open on Friday following a tech selloff on Wall Street and in Asia, as investors eyed the latest US non-farm payrolls report.

Ipek Ozkardeskaya, senior analyst at Swissquote, said: "The tech selloff accelerated yesterday, pushing the Nasdaq 100 down by an eye-watering 6.36%. The S&P 500 shed more than 4%, and the Korean Kospi is down by 5%. The memory-chip bubble there had already burst around June, with investors heading towards the exit all at the same time, as everyone wondered when the AI frenzy would come to an end. It is possible that we have reached boiling point in Nasdaq too, and now value has started evaporating.

"I hear hopes about Anthropic’s upcoming IPO, which could be delayed, by the way, if things get worse from here. The Nasdaq 100 is now in correction territory, having slid more than 10% from its October peak. The S&P 500 would join it if the selloff extends towards the 7,050 mark."

Looking to the rest of the day, attention will turn to the non-farm payrolls report for October, along with average earnings and the unemployment rate, due at 1330 GMT. Expectations are for 65,000 jobs to have been added in October, while the unemployment rate is set to remain at 4.2%.
On home shores, data released earlier showed that house prices slid in October as the challenging economic backdrop hit home.

The Lloyds house price index fell 0.6% last month, building on September’s 0.1% decline. On an annual basis, house prices are now 1.2% lower - the biggest fall since October 2023. The average property price is now £296,285.

sum: London's blue-chip index outperformed most global markets on Friday 30 October 2026, with pharmaceutical, telecoms and energy heavyweights cushioning a sharp fall in NatWest and a global technology selloff.

The FTSE 100 closed at 10,729.78 on Friday 30 October 2026, up 7.71 points or 0.07% from Thursday's close of 10,722.07. London's index opened higher and rose about 0.5% in the first hour of trade, according to InstaForex, before giving back most of that advance as the global technology selloff deepened and Wall Street opened sharply lower. The small gain was nonetheless enough to secure the FTSE 100's first monthly rise in three months.

The index's resilience stands out on a day when Japan's Nikkei 225 fell more than 2%, Nasdaq futures dropped more than 2% and Germany's DAX 40 retreated. The FTSE 100's heavy weighting toward pharmaceuticals, energy, consumer staples and mining, and its relatively light exposure to technology, has made it a natural refuge during the latest bout of AI-related selling.

AstraZeneca, one of the three largest companies in the index, was among the leading risers after reporting third-quarter revenue of $16,209 million, up 7% at constant exchange rates, and core earnings per share of $2.79, up 19% at constant exchange rates. The drugmaker reaffirmed its full-year guidance and announced a restructuring programme expected to save around $1.5 billion, which it said would support long-term ambitions including investment in new drug pipelines.

AstraZeneca shares closed about 7% higher, the stock's best day in a year according to Reuters reporting, and GSK added around 2.5%. The broader pharmaceutical sector gained 5.1% over October, its biggest monthly rise since February. Because AstraZeneca carries such a large index weighting, its rally alone more than offset the losses in banks and miners.

NatWest Group was the biggest drag on the index and the worst performer in the STOXX 600, closing nearly 9% lower after its third-quarter net interest income fell short of analyst expectations. The bank reported attributable profit of £1,532 million and operating pre-tax profit of £2.23 billion, up from £2.18 billion a year earlier, with total income of £4.64 billion.

sum: London's blue-chip index snapped a two-day losing streak, gapping higher at the open and holding its gains all day as Sage, RELX and the miners rallied, while Vodafone, BT and Airtel Africa fell after SpaceX moved into US mobile.

The FTSE 100 closed at 10,552.05 on Friday 9 October 2026, up 110.45 points or 1.06% from Thursday's close of 10,441.60. The gain ended a two-day losing streak that had pushed it to its lowest level since June. The index opened at 10,441.50, which proved to be the session low, and jumped above 10,520 within minutes of the start of trading. It then held a tight range through the morning before rising to a session high of 10,577.33 around 1 p.m. and closing near the upper end of the day's range.

The more domestically focused FTSE 250 also performed strongly, trading about 1.2% higher at midday. Friday's rally recovered all of the ground lost over Wednesday and Thursday, when rising oil prices and a surge in gilt yields had weighed on UK equities.

The common thread across Europe was a retreat in geopolitical risk. President Donald Trump said on Truth Social that the United States would not launch new strikes on Iran before the 3 November midterm elections and described talks with Tehran as productive. Brent crude, which had topped $105 a barrel on Thursday, fell to about $102.70 by midday, although prices recovered later in the session as Hurricane Isaias continued to curb more than 1.2 million barrels a day of Gulf of Mexico output. Lower oil prices eased pressure on government bonds, with France's 10-year yield falling about 7 basis points to 4.82% and Germany's 10-year Bund yield near 3.47%.

For UK markets, the bond backdrop mattered most. The 10-year gilt yield had reached 5.527% on Thursday, its highest level in 19 years, raising concern about government borrowing costs and mortgage rates. Signs of stabilisation in global bond markets on Friday gave investors room to buy interest-rate-sensitive and growth stocks again.
Software and data companies led the market. Sage Group rose more than 4% and RELX gained about 4%, with Experian up close to 4% during the session.

sum: FTSE 100 investors could be in for a bumpy ride. Trade-route disruptions and geopolitical conflicts are fuelling fears of a stock market correction, or even a full-blown crash. Yet Britain's flagship index remains near record highs.
So far, corporate earnings have proven remarkably resilient. But if disaster does strike, what should investors expect from UK large-cap stocks? Here's what history has to say.

During major meltdowns, geographic diversification offers surprisingly little protection. When the dotcom bubble burst, the financial crisis struck, and pandemic emerged, UK, EU, and US shares generally plunged together.
That's because panic's as contagious as an air-born virus. And the end result is companies were tossed out even if the underlying business remained strong.

However, during milder corrections, a different story often emerges. For example, in 2022, soaring inflation and rapidly rising interest rates hammered highly valued US tech stocks, dragging the S&P 500 down sharply along with the Nasdaq.

Yet the FTSE 100 actually finished the year slightly higher. Its heavier exposure to oil, mining, banking, healthcare and consumer staples provided far more protection versus America's technology-dominated market. And that continues to be true in 2026.

Even with efforts to build out AI data centres, the FTSE 100's direct exposure to the technology sector remains remarkably light. So if another tech bust were to emerge, UK shares could prove far more resilient, provided the sell-off doesn't cascade into a wider market panic attack.

sum: Aviva (LSE: AV) shares have done something other FTSE 100 stocks can only dream of: delivered bags of share price growth and dividend income too.
Over the last five years, the shares are up around 77%. During much of that time they’ve yielded around 6%-7%, lifting the total return comfortably beyond 100% with dividends reinvested.
Alas, I backed FTSE 100 rival Legal & General whose shares are up a pathetic 2.5% in five years, which serves to shed an even more positive light on Aviva.

After such a strong run, it was always likely Aviva shares would slow. They’re up a modest 6% over the last year. The trailing yield has slipped to about 5.5%, but that’s forecast to hit 5.8% in 2026 and 6.2% in 2027. So can Aviva deliver more growth and, crucially, keep the income flowing?

Latest results suggest Aviva hasn’t run out of steam yet. First-half 2026 operating profit jumped 24% to £1.3bn, while earnings per share rose 10% to 31.8p. Return on equity improved to 20.3% and cash remittances surged 47% to almost £1.5bn.

Wealth net flows were up 32%, while Aviva says it’s making good progress integrating its Direct Line acquisition. It also sees further potential in wealth, general insurance, health and protection, boosting by heavy AI invesment.
Group CEO Amanda Blanc talked up “six consecutive years of excellent financial performance, with much more to come”. Let’s hope she’s right.

items.t: Британские акции: простой способ заработать богатство?
sum: There are lots of ways people attempt and build wealth, from setting up their own business to investing in well-known blue-chip UK stocks.
Some wealth-building methods involve a lot of hard work, but buying shares on a regular basis over the long term does not.
There are lots of reasons to consider setting up your own business, but an easy life is not one of them. Entrepreneurship can be labour-intensive.

Share ownership can involve entrepreneurship too. But it is not the shareholder who has to do it. Rather, they can benefit from the hard work, business success and entrepreneurial flair of the companies in which they invest.
Of course, not all businesses do well and some that do are expensively priced on the stock market. So it takes some time to decide what UK stocks to buy when building a portfolio.
After that though, the investor can largely sit back and simply monitor their portfolio from time to time, while others do the all hard work.

Still, could investing in the stock market really help someone build substantial wealth? That depends how much they invest and what sort of annual return they achieve, between capital gain (or loss) and any dividends paid by the shares they own.

sum: The FTSE 350 is home to many iconic British businesses. And while I own shares in a few of them — such as Guinness maker Diageo, HSBC, and Rolls-Royce — I'm not superpatriotic enough to just invest in any, even if they look cheap.
Here are three iconic UK firms whose shares I'm giving a wide berth.
The first is FTSE 100 telecoms giant BT (LSE:BT.A). Well, I say giant, but today it's only the 34th largest company in the Footsie by market cap.
That's because BT hasn't done much growing. In fact, the stock's down 70% since mid-2015!

Annual revenue has remained in the £18bn-£20bn range for a long time, despite billions spent on fibre and 5G. It reminds me of that famous quote from Through the Looking-Glass: "It takes all the running you can do, to keep in the same place".

This lack of underlying growth has forced the group into multiple restructurings and rounds of layoffs to cut costs and try to improve profitability. The dividend was axed during the pandemic then rebased at half the prior rate.
Dividends were also cut during the dotcom crash and financial crisis, so it doesn't have a great track record of resilience during crises.

Futures traders have the FTSE 100 called 40 points lower, building on Thursday's 77-point decline to 10,639. The blue-chip index faces pressure from two directions: a sharp Wall Street sell-off driven by disappointing Big Tech earnings, and fresh geopolitical anxiety in the Middle East pushing oil prices to triple figures for the first time in months.

US stocks fell heavily overnight, with the Nasdaq leading the way down 2.2% as investors took a dim view of quarterly results from Alphabet and Tesla. The S&P 500 dropped 1.2%, its worst session of the month, while the Dow shed 1%.

The problem wasn't the earnings themselves, according to Swissquote's Ipek Ozkardeskaya; it was the spending. "Earnings themselves were not the problem; spending and evaporating free cash flow were," she said. sum: FTSE 100 mining and precious metals stocks came under significant selling pressure on Friday, May 15, with Fresnillo PLC [LSE: FRES], Antofagasta PLC [LSE: ANTO], Anglo American PLC [LSE: AAL], and Endeavour Mining PLC [LSE: EDV] among the index’s biggest fallers as gold slipped 1.4% to $4,586.42 an ounce and silver sank more than 6% to $78.26.

The FTSE 100 itself was trading down 1.18% at 10,250.93 by mid-morning according to Google Finance data, with the mining complex accounting for a meaningful portion of the decline as the index’s commodity-heavy composition amplified the sector’s losses.

The trigger was a sharp reversal in sentiment around the US-Iran conflict, following President Trump’s dismissal of Tehran’s latest peace proposal as a “piece of garbage,” combined with his warning that the ceasefire was on “life support,” statements that sent a relief rally building across metals and miners sharply into reverse.

The link between Iran and gold prices is more complex than a simple risk-off dynamic, and understanding it requires tracking the mechanics of the conflict’s impact on interest rate expectations rather than just its effect on sentiment.

When Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz earlier in 2026, oil surged past $100 a barrel, stoking inflation and forcing the Federal Reserve into a higher-for-longer stance on rates, which is toxic for gold as a non-yielding asset, and the metal duly sold off more than 25% from its January peak before recovering toward current levels.

With the peace deal stalling again on Friday, traders were repricing more of the same: higher oil, higher inflation, fewer or later rate cuts, and therefore a more hostile environment for gold prices regardless of the geopolitical anxiety the conflict also generates.

Global brokerages have already trimmed their 2026 rate cut forecasts in response to the inflation trajectory linked to the conflict, with some now pencilling in no cuts at all for the remainder of the year, a stark shift from the two to three cuts that were being priced at the start of 2026.

sum: European equities traded modestly higher on Thursday as investors monitored developments from the summit between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in Beijing, while continued enthusiasm surrounding artificial intelligence provided further support to technology stocks.
By 07:05 GMT, the pan-European Stoxx 600 index had gained 0.4%. Germany's DAX advanced 1.1%, France's CAC 40 rose 0.6%, while the UK's FTSE 100 traded broadly flat.

Technology shares remained among the strongest performers in Europe, following the positive momentum seen on Wall Street during the previous session. Companies including ASML (EU:ASML) and STMicroelectronics (BIT:STMMI) both moved higher as investor appetite for AI-related stocks continued to strengthen.

The first round of discussions between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping concluded during the opening phase of their two-day summit. According to Chinese state media, Xi said negotiations — particularly on trade — were progressing, although he also warned that disagreements over Taiwan could negatively affect relations between the two countries.

Markets were also watching closely for any signs of diplomatic discussions linked to the conflict involving Iran. Some analysts believe Trump may attempt to encourage China, one of the largest importers of Iranian crude oil, to support efforts aimed at securing a longer-term peace arrangement, although uncertainty remains over whether Beijing would be willing to take on such a role.

At the same time, investors continue to assess the economic risks associated with the prolonged disruption of the Strait of Hormuz, the key shipping route off Iran's southern coast through which around 20% of global oil supply passes.

Oil prices extended recent gains, with Brent crude trading above $105 per barrel compared with levels near $70 before the conflict escalated. The sharp rise in energy prices has increased concerns about renewed inflationary pressure globally, particularly after recent U.S. consumer and producer inflation data.

sum: LONDON — European markets declined on Monday as investors continued to monitor developments in the Middle East and a potential renewal of transatlantic trade tensions.

The pan-European Stoxx 600 closed 1% lower, reversing gains from earlier in the session. Major bourses in Frankfurt, Paris and Milan all closed in the red, while regional stocks were also largely negative. In London, the FTSE 100 was closed for the U.K. early spring bank holiday.
Nokia closed 7.4% higher, taking the Finnish telco's gains to more than 100% since the start of the year, after Inseego said Thursday it would acquire Nokia's fixed wireless access business.

European automakers tumbled after U.S. President Donald Trump said Friday he would increase tariffs on cars and trucks from the European Union to 25%. The European Commission said it was keeping its options in terms of its response.
Auto parts maker Continental slumped to the bottom of the Stoxx 600, falling 4.6% as Mercedes Benz shed 3.4% and Volkswagen lost more than 2%.
The new duty threat came despite a Supreme Court ruling in February striking down large parts of Trump's tariff agenda.

Meanwhile, President Trump also unveiled a new plan to "free" ships that have been unable to pass through the Strait of Hormuz. The initiative, dubbed "Project Freedom," could involve 15,000 troops, guided missile destroyers, and 100 aircraft guiding commercial ships through the critical shipping channel, according to a social media post from U.S. Central Command.

sum: - This ETF provides exposure to the largest 100 companies in the UK

An ETF is a basket of investments that often includes shares or bonds. They tend to track the performance of an index such as the FTSE 100 and trade on stock exchanges, like shares. This means their price fluctuates throughout the day.

The iShares Core FTSE 100 ETF invests in the 100 largest companies in the UK. While the FTSE 100 is a UK index, many of the companies also earn money overseas. Investors will therefore be indirectly investing into foreign economies as well as the UK.

An ETF is one of the simplest ways to invest and can be a low-cost starting point for an investment portfolio aiming to deliver long-term growth. This ETF could be used to diversify a global portfolio, or one focused on smaller companies or other investments such as bonds.

sum: Tesco (LSE:TSCO) shares have performed tremendously over the past five years, roughly doubling the FTSE 100‘s return. But the supermarket stock has pulled back by approximately 8% in the past month.
Does this leave Tesco attractive from a dividend and share price target perspective? Let’s take a look at the latest broker forecasts.
The average 12-month share price target among 12 City analysts is currently 491p. That’s only around 6% higher than the present price, suggesting Tesco might be fairly valued.
Encouragingly though, the 15 brokers giving the stock a rating in the past three months have it down as a Buy. Five rate it a Hold, none a Sell.
A price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 20 seems a little on the high side. But looking ahead, the forward P/E multiple drops to a more reasonable 15.

This is still above rivals J Sainsbury (13.3) and Marks and Spencer (10), but Tesco’s market share is hovering close to 29%, its highest in more than a decade. So it arguably deserves a premium valuation, especially with slightly higher profit margins.

Turning to income, the forward dividend yield is 3.4%. That’s above the FTSE 100 average, but there’s not much in it. An investor putting £5,000 into the stock would be hoping to get around £170 back in dividends.

Crucially, previous assumptions that a period of modest inflation and further interest rate cuts is ahead could prove to be grossly misplaced. Oil and gas prices have spiked over recent weeks in response to conflict in the Middle East. This could ultimately filter through to higher-than-expected rates of inflation across developed economies over the coming months, which prompts central banks to adopt a more cautious attitude towards monetary policy easing.

In fact, the Bank of England was previously expected to reduce interest rates at its March meeting but decided to hold them at 3.75% in response to the potential for higher-than-expected inflation. Further caution from policymakers across developed markets over the short run may mean that tighter, rather than looser, monetary policy results. This would be unhelpful for the world economy’s near-term growth rate and the short-term outlook for the FTSE 350 Industrial Support Services sector.

Of course, an uncertain near-term economic outlook and the lower share prices it brings can present excellent long-term buying opportunities for investors. Cheaper stocks provide scope to purchase high-quality companies at more attractive prices than would normally be the case. This allows for the prospect of sizeable upward re-ratings to earnings multiples that can have a material impact on capital returns over the long run.

With regards to industrial support services members, the sector’s poor performance over recent years means that, in some cases, they were already trading at appealing prices even prior to the war in Iran. Indeed, the sector is down 6% over the past five years. This compares to a 39% rise for the FTSE 350 index over the same period, with challenges such as a global trade war weighing on the sector’s performance, especially over recent months.

Iran remains in a strong position. It retains control of the Strait of Hormuz as leverage over the US and its allies, forcing the US to recalibrate. Clearly, Trump’s prime objective is no longer regime change but to reopen the Strait. Did any of his advisers recall how the Suez Canal was shut for eight years following the 1967 Six-Day War?

Urgency was underlined just before this surprise turn of events by a chief of the International Energy Agency (IEA) declaring this crisis as “equivalent to the combined force of the twin oil shocks of the 1970s plus the fallout of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine on the gas market”. It would compromise “vital arteries of the global economy”, including petrochemicals, fertilisers and helium – an essential aspect for microchips and artificial intelligence (AI) besides hospitals.

sum: It was no surprise, when equity markets first reacted to news of the strikes on Iran, that the U.K.'s FTSE 100 fell by less than all of its major continental European peers.
What is often seen as the Footsie's weakness — its defensive assortment of pharmaceutical, utility, tobacco and consumer goods stocks — comes into its own at times of market volatility.

Additionally, the index contains plenty of constituents likely to benefit from turmoil in the Middle East, such as the defense contractor BAE Systems and suppliers to the industry, like Babcock International, Rolls-Royce and Melrose Industries, as well as oil majors BP and Shell.

This is a pattern well-established during times of strife: during the second Iraq War in 2003 and the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks in the U.S., the Footsie outperformed its European peers and, during the latter, the Dow Jones Industrial Average as well.

Mining stocks, which could benefit from higher commodity prices caused by disruption to shipping routes and supply chains, are also well represented in the FTSE 100. Rio Tinto, Glencore, Anglo American and the Chilean copper miner Antofagasta are among the 20 largest stocks in the index, while the likes of Fresnillo and Endeavour Mining are well-placed to benefit should the uncertainty lead to another leg higher in the price of gold.

Nor do these defensive qualities apply just to the leading 100 U.K.-listed companies. The FTSE 250, the mid-cap U.K. stock index, is replete with defense industry suppliers, including Qinetiq Group, Avon Technologies, Hunting and Senior, not to mention oil and gas plays such as Ithaca Energy, Harbour Energy and Clarkson, the world's largest shipbroking and integrated shipping services provider, another likely beneficiary from maritime disruption.
So, for investors seeking to retain exposure to equities during times of conflict in the Middle East, the U.K. stock market is not a bad option.
